Death of a Salesman. Arthur Miller's tragedy follows Willy Loman, an aging traveling salesman whose mental and financial decline culminates in suicide. Through fragmented scenes mixing past and present, the play explores the collision between Willy's delusional faith in the American Dream and the harsh realities of capitalism and human limitation.

The play premiered on Broadway in 1949 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama that year. It has become one of the most frequently performed American plays. Willy's final act is suicide by car crash, designed to make it look accidental so his family can collect insurance money. The character Biff, Willy's favorite son, was expected to succeed but became a drifter. Their relationship fragments over Biff's discovery of Willy's infidelity. The play is staged without a conventional set. The playwright used lighting and sound design to shift between Willy's present humiliation and memories of his past ambitions.

The play introduced the term anti-hero to American drama. Willy is not admirable but sympathetic, undone by forces larger than himself. Happy, Willy's younger son, remains trapped in his father's delusional worldview, promising to vindicate Willy's failing legacy. Arthur Miller's work stands as his response to post-war American capitalism and moral compromise. The American Dream is the play's central theme, shown as a trap and delusion rather than an aspirational ideal.

Tennessee Williams is a contemporary playwright exploring similar themes of desperation and false promise in American life. The Crucible is Miller's other major work, also examining scapegoating and moral reckoning. The Great Gatsby dissects the mythology of American success and desire. The play asks profound questions about what we sacrifice for our ambitions and what we owe to those we love.
